It says he lived a thousand years before Nūḥ and was among his ancestors (Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī, with reference to Mustadrak al-Ḥākim); that he was the first Prophet after Ādam, and that Allah bestowed upon him thirty books (Abī Dharr–Zamakhsharī, as the commentary cites it); that he was the first man given the knowledge of astrology and mathematics, through a miracle (Baḥr ul-Muḥīṭ); that he was the first man who learned how to write with a pen, the first who invented the stitching of cloth — people wore animal skins instead of clothes before his time — and the first to invent measurement tools; and that the making of weapons also began in his time, which he used in his wars, the Holy wars — *jihād* — against the descendants of Qābīl (Baḥr ul-Muḥīṭ, Qurṭubī, Mazharī, Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī).

## "And We raised him to a high station" — what the scholars said, and where they stopped

Here the commentators genuinely differ, and it is worth seeing the range rather than being handed one answer.

- **Mujāhid** — reported by Sufyān from Manṣūr — said the high station means **the fourth heaven**. Ibn Kathir connects this to what is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by Idrīs on the night of the Isrāʾ (the Night Journey), and he was in the fourth heaven.
- **Al-Ḥasan and others** said it means **Paradise**.
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** reads it as rank: that he was granted a special position among the prophets and was close to Allah.

On the other versions about his ascent to the sky, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Ibn Kathir's verdict that this material is taken from the traditions of the Israelites as reported by Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, some of which are disputed and unfamiliar.

Its own conclusion is a model of scholarly restraint, and worth quoting in substance: the Qur'anic words are not specific on the subject of whether he was given a sublime position or was physically lifted to the sky. His physical ascent is therefore not definite — and in any case, commentary of the Qur'an is not dependent on this issue (Bayān ul-Qurʼān).

That is the discipline these two portraits invite. Where Allah speaks, we affirm: He raised Idrīs to a high station, and He was pleased with Ismāʿīl. Where He is silent about the mechanics, we do not fill the silence.

## Living it

Four things this passage asks of a believer, all of them within reach:

1. **Let your word be a debt.** Not enforceable in court, and therefore entirely a matter of your relationship with Allah. Break it without a religious excuse and you have sinned — this is the jurists' position as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports it.
2. **Watch the three signs.** Lying when you speak, breaking what you promise, betraying what you are trusted with — Ibn Kathir's inference stands: the true believer is defined by behaving contrary to all three.
3. **Start at home.** Ṣalāh and Zakāh, enjoined on your own household first, with patience (20:132) and without neglect. And build the environment, because that is what actually forms people.
4. **Aim past reward.** The ayah's final word about Ismāʿīl is that his Lord was pleased with him. That is the target.

passages.title: The prophets' heirs: prayer neglected, the Gardens regained
passages.tafsir:
Ibn Kathīr marks the turn that shapes this passage: after Allah mentions the party of the blessed — the prophets, and those who followed them by keeping the limits Allah set — He then mentions those who succeeded them. Ayah 58 shows the prophets in worship; ayah 59 shows the successors who lost the prayer and followed desires; ayah 60 leaves the door of return open; ayat 61–63 describe the Gardens the returners walk into. The thread running through all six is **inheritance** — what is handed down, what is squandered, and what is finally given.

## Ayah 58: the family tree of guidance

The ayah gathers the prophets under one sentence — "Those were they unto whom Allah bestowed His grace from among the Prophets" — then traces them through four channels of descent. As-Suddī and Ibn Jarīr, quoted by Ibn Kathīr, map them out: **"of the offspring of Ādam"** is Idrīs; **"of those whom We carried with Nūḥ"** is Ibrāhīm; **"of the offspring of Ibrāhīm"** is Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb and Ismāʿīl; **"of Isrāʾīl"** is Mūsā, Hārūn, Zakariyyā, Yaḥyā and ʿĪsā son of Maryam. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān gives the same breakdown.

Why the careful sorting, when Ādam fathers every one of them? Ibn Jarīr answers that this is the distinction of their genealogies — because one among them was not a descendant of those on the ship with Nūḥ, and that is Idrīs, for he was Nūḥ's grandfather. Ibn Kathīr says: "this is the most apparent meaning, which concludes that Idrīs is amongst the pillars of Nūḥ's ancestral lineage."

Ibn Kathīr then widens the ayah: **the praise is not confined to the prophets named in this sūrah.** Rather it refers to all of those who were prophets. He supports this with the parallel roll-call of Sūrah al-Anʿām (6:83–87), which names Nūḥ, Dāwūd, Sulaymān, Ayyūb, Yūsuf, Ilyās, al-Yasaʿ, Yūnus and Lūṭ alongside the others, and adds "some of their fathers and their progeny and their brethren" — and with Allah's words, "Of some of them We have related to you their story. And of some We have not related to you their story" (40:78).

## Prostrate and weeping — and why it comes exactly here

The ayah ends: "When the Ayāt of the Most Gracious were recited unto them, they fell down prostrate and weeping."

Ibn Kathīr explains: when they heard the Words of Allah, mentioning His proofs and evidences, they prostrated to their Lord in humility, humbleness, praise and thanks for the great favours they were blessed with. **Bukiyyan** means those who are crying; it is the plural of *bākin*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws out why this comes at precisely this moment, quoting Bayān ul-Qurʾān: some very prominent prophets have just been mentioned along with their exalted status, so there was a real danger that people might raise them to an exaggerated position — as the Jews did with Sayyidnā ʿUzayr (عليه السلام), and the Christians with Sayyidnā ʿĪsā (عليه السلام). Therefore the very next thing said of them is that they were all deeply reverent before Allah and used to prostrate to Him in extreme reverence — to close off any possibility of crossing the limits of reverence for them. The remedy for exaggerating a prophet is to watch him worship.

**This is a verse of prostration.** Ibn Kathīr states that, because of this, the scholars agree it is legislated to prostrate upon reading this ayah — in *following* the prophets and adhering to their manner of worship. He cites a report in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī: Mujāhid asked Ibn ʿAbbās, "Is there a prostration in Sūrah Ṣād?" Ibn ʿAbbās replied, "Yes," then recited "They are those whom Allah had guided. So follow their guidance" (6:90), and said: "So your Prophet is one of those who have been commanded to follow them. And he is of those who should be followed" — referring to Dāwūd.

**Weeping over the Qurʾān is prophetic practice.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes it is a commendable act and an attribute of the prophets; it has been reported that the Prophet ﷺ, his Companions, their followers and the pious followed this practice. From Qurṭubī it adds that religious scholars consider it desirable, when going into a recitation-prostration, to recite a supplication appropriate to that verse — and for *this* verse: *"O Allah, make me of those among Your slaves upon whom You bestowed Your bounties, who prostrate before You, who weep while reciting Your verses."*

## Ayah 59: the successors who let the prayer fall

"Then, there has succeeded them a posterity who have lost the Ṣalāh and have followed lusts."

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, citing Mazharī, points to a fine distinction: **khalf** means *bad* successors, while **khalaf** means *good* successors. Ibn Kathīr glosses the phrase simply as later generations. Maʿārif adds Mujāhid's report that when the Day of Judgement draws near and the pious people have all died away, people will lose interest in prayers and indulge in all sorts of vices. Note the sequence: prayer neglected *first*, desires followed *after*.

### What "losing the prayer" actually means

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān lays out three positions:

1. **Praying after the time has lapsed** — the view of most exegetes, among them Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, Nakhaʿī, Qāsim, Mujāhid, Ibrāhīm and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.
2. **Any lapse in the form and conditions of the prayer**, with the lapse of time included in that.
3. **Praying at home rather than with the congregation** (Qurṭubī, Baḥr ul-Muḥīṭ).

Maʿārif states plainly that offering prayers outside the fixed time, or not with the congregation, is a default and of no avail, and is a great sin.

Ibn Kathīr preserves the same discussion. He first gives the sense that losing their prayers is when they *do not consider the prayers obligatory* — and comments that they therefore lose, "because the prayer is the pillar and foundation of the religion. It is the best of the servants' deeds." Such people then occupy themselves with worldly desires and delights, pleased with the life of this world.

But he then reports the salaf insisting on a narrower reading. Al-Qāsim ibn Mukhaymirah said it means they will not keep up with the proper times of the prayer, because if it meant complete abandonment of the prayer, this would be disbelief. Ibn Masʿūd was once addressed about the Qurʾān's many mentions of prayer — "Those who neglect their Ṣalāh" (107:5), "Those who remain constant in their Ṣalāh" (70:23), "Who guard their Ṣalāh" (23:9). He said: **"This means at its designated times."** The people said, "We thought that this was referring to the abandonment of the prayer." He replied, "That would be disbelief." Masrūq said: "No one who guards the five daily prayers will be written among the heedless. In their neglect is destruction. Their neglect is delaying them past their fixed times." ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz recited this very ayah and said their loss was not their abandonment of the prayers, but not offering them during their proper and prescribed times.

So the ayah is not describing distant unbelievers. It describes people who still pray — late, hurried, careless — and calls that *losing* it.

### How seriously the early Muslims took this

- Sayyidnā **ʿUmar al-Fārūq** ؓ sent a circular to all his governors: *"In my view the most important among your tasks is prayer. So, whoever defaults in this, will default in discharging his other obligations all the more."* (Muwaṭṭaʾ Imām Mālik)
- Sayyidnā **Ḥudhayfah** ؓ once saw a man praying without observing the prescribed rules, rushing through the rituals without pausing, and asked how long he had been praying that way. Forty years, the man said. Ḥudhayfah told him, *"You have not offered a single of your prayers correctly"* — and added that if he died praying like this, he would die without following the course given by the Prophet ﷺ.
- Sayyidnā **Abū Masʿūd** ؓ has been quoted in **Tirmidhī** that the Prophet ﷺ said the prayer of a person is lost who does not observe *iqāmah* — who does not stand upright in his prayer. Maʿārif explains: if one does not pause in *rukūʿ* and *sujūd*, does not stand straight up after bowing, or does not sit up between the two prostrations, the prayer is considered as not performed; likewise, carelessness about *wuḍūʾ* and cleanliness loses it.
- **Ḥasan al-Baṣrī** (رح) observed that leaving the mosques unattended and being over-involved in business and the enjoyments of life is included in the meaning of this verse.
- **Imām Qurṭubī** (رح) remarked that even knowledgeable people ignore the prescribed rules of prayer and merely go through its motions — and he wrote that in the sixth century Hijrah, when such people were few. Maʿārif observes that the position today is worse.

### "And followed desires"

Maʿārif defines **shahawāt** as all those worldly pleasures which make people negligent of their duty to Allah and make them lose interest in prayer. Sayyidnā ʿAlī ؓ, as Qurṭubī reports, named examples: palatial houses, luxurious carriages that attract people's eye, and clothing worn to distinguish oneself from the common man. The criterion is not the thing itself but what it does to a person.

### *Ghayy* — what they will meet

As a word: Maʿārif explains that *ghayy* is the opposite of *rashād* — all virtues and good things are *rashād*, and all vices and evils are *ghayy*. Among the early authorities Ibn Kathīr cites, Ibn ʿAbbās said it means **loss**, and Qatādah said **evil**; Ibn Kathīr himself glosses it as loss on the Day of Resurrection.

As a place: Ibn Kathīr reports from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd that it is a valley in the Hellfire which is very deep and whose food is filthy; Abū ʿIyāḍ said it is a valley in Hell made of pus and blood. Maʿārif reports from Ibn Masʿūd ؓ that there is a cave in Hell by the name of *Ghayy* which houses various types of severe punishments, more numerous than all the punishments of Hell — and from Ibn ʿAbbās ؓ, via Qurṭubī, that even Hell seeks protection from it, and that Allah has prepared it for habitual adulterers, drunkards who do not give up drinking, usurers who do not stop taking interest, those who disobey their parents, those who give false witness, and the woman who declares someone else's child as her husband's.

## Ayah 60: the exception that reopens everything

**"Except those who repent and believe and work righteousness. Such will enter Paradise and they will not be wronged in aught."**

Ibn Kathīr reads it precisely: except those who **recant** from giving up the prayers and following the desires — for Allah will accept their repentance, give them a good end, and make them of those who inherit the Garden of Delight.

Then he explains the closing promise with a principle: **repentance wipes away that which was before it.** The Prophet ﷺ said, "The one who repents from sin is like he who has no sin." Because of this, Ibn Kathīr says, those who repent will not lose anything from the good deeds they did; they will not be held accountable for what they did before their repentance in a way that decreases their reward for the deeds they do after it, because whatever they did before repenting is lost, forgotten and not taken to account. He calls this "an honour from the Most Generous and a kindness from the Most Gentle," and notes the same pattern in Sūrah al-Furqān, where grave sins are listed and then excepted for those who repent, closing "and Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (25:68–70).

The frightening description in ayah 59 was never a sentence passed; it was a warning issued with an exit clearly marked.

## Ayat 61–62: what the returners walk into

**"Gardens of ʿAdn."** Ibn Kathīr: the Gardens which the penitent will enter will be Gardens of ʿAdn — *meaning, eternity.*

**"which the Most Gracious has promised to His servants in the unseen."** Ibn Kathīr notes that these Gardens are among the unseen things they *believe in, even though they have never witnessed them* — out of their strong conviction and the strength of their faith. And note the name Allah uses of Himself here — **ar-Raḥmān**, the Most Gracious — the same name whose āyāt made the prophets fall prostrate and weeping in ayah 58.

**"Verily, His promise must come to pass."** Ibn Kathīr says this affirms that it will occur and that it is a settled matter: Allah does not break His promise, nor does He change it, as in "His promise is certainly to be accomplished" (73:18). On the word *maʾtiyyan* he gives two readings: that it will **come to** His servants who are striving towards it, and they will reach it; and the reading of other commentators that coming and being come to are two faces of one thing — as the Arabs say, "Fifty years came to me," and "I came to fifty years," both meaning the same.

**"They shall not hear therein any *laghw*, but only *salām*."** Ibn Kathīr: in these gardens there is no ignorant, wasteful and useless speech, like there is in this life. Maʿārif defines *laghw* as idle, absurd, frivolous and abusive talk. Ibn Kathīr calls the exception *"an indifferent exception"* — *salām* is not a variety of *laghw* being carved out — as in "No laghw will they hear therein, nor any sinful speech. But only the saying of: Salām! Salām!" (56:25–26). Maʿārif adds, from Qurṭubī, that whatever one hears there will add to his happiness, peace and tranquillity, including the customary greetings the dwellers of Paradise exchange among themselves and those the angels offer them.

**"And they will have therein their sustenance, morning and afternoon."** Ibn Kathīr is careful: this means in what is *similar* to mornings and evenings; it does not mean there is night and day in Paradise, but that they will be living in times that alternate, knowing its lighted times from its lights and illumination. Ibn ʿAbbās, as ad-Ḍaḥḥāk reported, said it means the amount of time equal to night and day. Maʿārif agrees — no solar system, no rising or setting sun, but perpetual radiance with some way of telling morning from evening — and adds two explanations from Qurṭubī: that morning and evening are mentioned because of people's habit of eating and drinking at those hours, and by an Arab saying that whoever gets a full meal morning and evening is comfortable and at peace; and that other scholars take it as a general expression, like day and night or east and west, specifying no particular time — meaning they will get their provisions according to their choice at any time they like, in line with "and for themselves, there is what they desire" (16:57). Sayyidnā Anas ibn Mālik ؓ said, after reciting this verse, that it shows the believers have their meals twice a day.

Ibn Kathīr brings two narrations here. Imām Aḥmad recorded from Abū Hurayrah — and al-Bukhārī and Muslim both recorded it in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said the first group to enter Paradise will have forms like the form of the moon on a night when it is full; they will not spit, blow their noses or defecate therein; their containers and combs will be of gold and silver, their sweat the fragrance of musk; and **they will not have any disputes between them, or any hatred — their hearts united like the heart of one man, glorifying Allah in the morning and evening.** And Imām Aḥmad alone recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet ﷺ said the martyrs will be upon the banks of a river by the gates of Paradise, under a green dome, their sustenance brought out to them from Paradise, morning and evening.

## Ayah 63: what is inherited, and by whom

"Such is the Paradise which We shall give as an inheritance to those of Our servants who had **taqwā**."

Ibn Kathīr: this Paradise, described with these magnificent attributes, is what Allah will cause His pious servants to inherit. And he tells us who they are — **those who obey Allah in happiness and in times of hardship, who suppress their anger, and who pardon people's offences.** *Taqwā* here is obedience that does not depend on circumstances, plus a mastery over the self at the moment of being wronged.

He closes by linking the ayah to the opening of Sūrah al-Muʾminūn: "Successful indeed are the believers. Those who are humble in their Ṣalāh" (23:1–2) … "These are indeed the inheritors. Who shall inherit al-Firdaws. In it they shall dwell forever" (23:10–11).

That closes the circle. Ayah 59 describes people who **lost** the prayer and so meet loss. Ayah 63 describes people who **inherit** — and the passage Ibn Kathīr reaches for to identify them begins with humility in prayer.

## Living it

**Guard the times.** On the reading of Ibn Masʿūd, Masrūq, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and most exegetes, "losing the prayer" is the habit of letting the window slip — a diagnosable, fixable thing.

**Guard the shape.** Abū Masʿūd's report in Tirmidhī puts stillness at the centre: pause in the bowing, stand straight up after it, sit up between the two prostrations, and do not be careless about wuḍūʾ. Ḥudhayfah's forty-year lesson is that long practice alone does not make a sound prayer.

**Watch what is pulling.** Maʿārif's test: which pleasures are making you negligent of your duty to Allah and draining your interest in prayer.

**Come back.** Ayah 60 is the mercy of this passage: if prayers have been lost for years, the door is repentance with faith and righteous action, and what preceded the repentance is lost, forgotten and not taken to account.

**Prostrate when you reach ayah 58**, and make there the supplication Qurṭubī recommended for it.

passages.title: The angels descend only by Allah's command
passages.tafsir:
Ayat 64–65 answer a private grief with a lesson about how the heavens work. In ayah 64 the words are spoken in the voice of the **angels** — "we descend not except by the command of your Lord" — and they add that everything before them, behind them and in between belongs to Allah, who never forgets. Ayah 65 draws the conclusion: the One who owns all of that is Lord of the heavens and the earth, so worship Him, persevere in that worship, and know that there is none like Him. What holds the two ayat together is a single movement — from *delay is not neglect* to *so worship Him*.

## The moment behind the words

Ibn Kathir heads his comment on this passage with the sentence that fixes its subject: **"The Angels do not descend, except by Allah's Command."** Then he tells us why that needed saying.

He reports that **Imam Ahmad recorded** that Ibn 'Abbas said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Jibril:

> "What prevents you from visiting us more than you do?"

— and then this ayah was revealed. Ibn Kathir adds a note on who carried the report: **al-Bukhari was alone in recording it**, and he related it with the Tafsir of this very ayah.

Alongside it Ibn Kathir gives a second report, from al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas:

> "Jibril was kept from visiting the Messenger of Allah, so he was disturbed and grieved because of this. Then Jibril came to him and said, 'O Muhammad: *And we descend not except by the command of your Lord.*'"

Sit with that scene for a moment. The visits from Jibril had been held back, and the Prophet ﷺ felt their absence — the report says plainly that he was **disturbed and grieved**. The question he puts to Jibril is almost tender: *why don't you come to us more often?*

And the reply, when it comes, is revelation itself. It does not say "you were wrong to miss me." It does not even say "I will come more often." It re-describes the whole arrangement: **the angels are not free agents.** Notice who is speaking here. Ibn Kathir's heading names the subject as the angels, and in al-'Awfi's report it is Jibril himself who brings these words to the Prophet ﷺ — a statement the angels make about their own condition. They do not come down on their own initiative, at their own pace, for their own reasons. They descend **by the command of your Lord** — and by nothing else.

That is the key that unlocks the passage. What looks from below like silence or absence is, from above, simply an order not yet given.

## "What is before us and what is behind us"

The ayah goes on: *To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us, and what is between those two* (ayah 64). Ibn Kathir records that the early authorities read this in two ways, and he reports both without forcing them into one.

**The first reading.** Ibn Kathir introduces its opening half anonymously — *"It has been said"* — that "what is before us" refers to **that which is in this life** and "what is behind us" refers to **the Hereafter**. He does not name anyone for that part. It is for the third phrase, *"and what is between those two,"* that he gives a named explanation: it means **what is between the two blows of the Ṣūr** — the Trumpet. That, he says, is the opinion of **Abu al-'Aliyah, 'Ikrimah and Mujahid**; it was also stated by **Sa'id bin Jubayr and Qatadah** in one narration from them; and **as-Suddi and ar-Rabi' bin Anas** held this opinion as well.

**The second reading.** This too Ibn Kathir opens with *"It has also been said"*: "what is before us" means **the future matters of the Hereafter**; "what is behind us" means **what has taken place in this life**; and "what is between those two" means **what happens between this life and the Hereafter**. He then reports that a statement like this explanation has come from **Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id bin Jubayr, ad-Dahhak, Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj and ath-Thawri**, and that **Ibn Jarir preferred this latter interpretation**. Ibn Kathir closes the discussion with the scholar's honest formula: *and Allah knows best.*

Notice that the two readings differ over which direction is "before" and which is "behind," but they agree entirely on the point being made. However you slice time — this life, the Hereafter, and the stretch in between that no living person has seen — **all of it belongs to Him.** The angels are not merely saying "we obey." They are saying: the One who commands us is the One to whom every stretch of time on both sides of us belongs, and the part we cannot see from here. He alone knows when a descent is due.

## "And your Lord is never forgetful"

Then the ayah lands its gentlest blow: **وَمَا كَانَ رَبُّكَ نَسِيًّا** — *and your Lord is never forgetful.*

Ibn Kathir gives **Mujahid's** gloss on it, and it is the whole point: **"This means that your Lord has not forgotten you."**

The sentence is phrased as a general truth about Allah — forgetfulness is simply not among His attributes — but Mujahid reads it as aimed at one grieving heart. We affirm this of Allah exactly as He affirmed it of Himself: He does not forget, without our likening Him to creation and without explaining the words away. And Mujahid draws out what the Prophet ﷺ most needed to hear from it. A pause in Jibril's visits could feel like being overlooked. Allah closes that door: **the delay was decree, not oversight.**

## Ayah 65: the ground of the command

Ayah 65 opens by widening the frame all the way out: **Lord of the heavens and the earth, and all that is between them.**

Ibn Kathir unpacks that title in four moves. Allah:

- **created** all of that;
- is the **Disposer of its affairs**;
- is the **Legislator over it**;
- and is in **absolute control of it, having no one to oppose His decisions**.

Read that back against ayah 64 and the logic clicks. The angels said *we descend only by His command*; ayah 65 says *and He is the One who made, runs, rules and legislates for everything between the heavens and the earth, with no one able to contest what He decides.* Of course the angels wait for His word. Everything waits for His word.

## "So worship Him, and persevere in His worship"

Now comes the response the passage asks for: **فَاعْبُدْهُ وَاصْطَبِرْ لِعِبَادَتِهِ**.

The ayah's own wording puts the command *after* the description: Lord of the heavens and the earth and all that is between them — **so worship Him.** Worship is where the passage lands. The answer to waiting on Allah is not to stop worshipping until the answer comes. It is to worship.

And the second verb carries more weight than the first. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stops on the word **اِصْطِبَار (iṣṭibār)** and gives its sense: **"perseverance in the face of acute distress and hardship."** The commentary then states the practical point without softening it: anyone who wishes to be constant and steadfast in his prayers must be prepared to undergo pain and suffering.

That is a realistic word about worship, and it is worth hearing. The ayah does not promise that steady devotion will feel easy or arrive on a wave of enthusiasm. It uses a word built for holding on under strain, and it tells the worshipper in advance: **expect the difficulty, and stay anyway.**

## "Do you know of any who is similar to Him?"

The passage ends with a question: **هَلْ تَعْلَمُ لَهُ سَمِيًّا** — *Do you know of any samiyy for Him?* The sources give two complementary explanations of that word.

**One: no equal, no comparison.** Ibn Kathir reports that 'Ali bin Abi Talhah related that **Ibn 'Abbas** explained it as, "Do you know any comparison or something similar to the Lord?" — and that **Mujahid, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj and others all said the same.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says many commentators hold this view, naming among them **Mujahid, Ibn Zubair, Qatadah and Ibn 'Abbas**, and puts the meaning like this: in the entire pantheon of false gods, **none is equal or comparable to Allah in so far as the divine attributes are concerned.**

This is the ordinary belief of Ahl al-Sunnah stated in a single question. Whatever Allah has affirmed of Himself, we affirm — and the moment we start picturing it as a creature's version of the same thing, this ayah cuts across us: *do you know anyone like Him?*

**Two: no one bears His name.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that in its generally accepted sense the word **samiyy** applies to **persons bearing the same name**, and then makes a striking observation. The polytheists and idolaters had included many humans, angels, stones and idols along with Allah in their worship, and designated all of them as objects of worship. Yet — the commentary calls it a strange and extraordinary coincidence — **not one of their false gods was ever named "Allah."** This, it says, was preordained: no idol or deity bore the name. So the literal reading works perfectly well here too — **there is no object in the world bearing Allah's name.**

Ibn Kathir carries the same idea to another of the divine names. 'Ikrimah related that **Ibn 'Abbas** said: **"There is no one named ar-Rahman — the Most Beneficent — other than Him, Blessed and Exalted is He. Most Holy is His Name."**

So the passage that began with the angels explaining their own limits ends by placing Allah beyond all comparison: no equal in the divine attributes, and not even a shared name.

## Living it

These two ayat are unusually practical for a passage about angels.

**Delay is not abandonment.** If the Prophet ﷺ could feel the ache of heaven's silence and be answered with *your Lord has not forgotten you*, then the believer whose du'a has not yet been answered has something to hold onto here. Nothing descends early; nothing descends late. It descends **by His command**.

**Nothing in your life arrives on its own initiative.** If Jibril himself does not choose his errands, then no good, and no hardship, reaches you outside the command of the One to whom what is before you, what is behind you, and what lies between all belong.

**The prescribed response to waiting is worship, not withdrawal.** Ayah 65 does not say "so be patient until He answers." It says **worship Him** — and hold on in that worship with iṣṭibār, the endurance that expects strain. Maʿārif's warning is the useful, unglamorous part: if you want your prayer to be constant, budget for the difficulty in advance.

**And take your need to the One with no equal.** The last question of the passage quietly redirects the heart. When you are waiting for something to come down to you, there is no second address to try — *do you know of any who is similar to Him?*

passages.title: Mocking resurrection, and the passage over Hell
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

Man throws out a sneer — *when I am dead, shall I then be raised up alive?* — and the rest of the passage is Allah's reply. First an answer drawn from man's own beginning (ayah 67), then a sworn answer (ayah 68), and then, instead of further argument, a scene: everyone brought to their knees around Hell, the worst in rebellion dragged out first, not one person exempt from passing over the Fire, and finally those who had *taqwā* saved while the wrongdoers are left kneeling where they were (ayat 69–72).

What holds the unit together is that movement from a taunt to a place. Man speaks once; after that Allah acts, verb after verb — *We shall gather*, *We shall bring them*, *We shall drag out*, *We know best*, *We shall save*, *We shall leave*. The question "will I be raised?" is answered not only with a proof but with the destination itself.

## The sneer, and the proof in his own beginning (66–67)

The sentence immediately before this passage had asked, **هَلْ تَعْلَمُ لَهُ سَمِيًّا** — "Do you know any one worthy of His name?" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that although the idolaters gave the status of deity to humans, angels, stones and idols, not one of their false gods was ever named Allah; and that many commentators — Mujāhid, Ibn Zubayr, Qatādah, Ibn ʿAbbās — take the word *samiyy* here to mean "a like" or "comparable": in that whole pantheon none is equal or comparable to Allah in His divine attributes. That is the backdrop against which *man says…*

Ibn Kathir opens by naming the attitude exactly: Allah, the Exalted, informs that mankind is **amazed** that he could be returned to life after death, and thinks this is something farfetched. It is not really a question; it is disbelief wearing the shape of a question. Ibn Kathir gathers the Qur'an's other portraits of the same voice — "And if you wonder, then wondrous is their saying: 'When we are dust, shall we indeed then be (raised) in a new creation?'" (13:5); and the man who "puts forth for Us a parable and forgets his own creation," asking "Who will give life to these bones after they are rotten and have become dust?" — to whom the answer comes, "He will give life to them Who created them for the first time! And He is the All-Knower of every creation!" (36:77–79).

The reply in our ayah works the same way. As Ibn Kathir puts it, **Allah uses the beginning of creation as a proof for its repetition**: He created the human being while he was *nothing* — so can He not repeat this creation after the human has actually become something? The Qur'an states the principle plainly elsewhere: "And He it is Who originates the creation, then He will repeat it; and this is easier for Him" (30:27).

So the mocker treats the second creation as the incredible one, while the ayah points him back to the first — and 30:27 calls the second the easier of the two. What he has forgotten, in the words of 36:78, is "his own creation."

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites a hadith recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ related that Allah, the Exalted, said: *"The son of Adam denies Me and he has no right to deny Me. The son of Adam harms Me and he has no right to harm Me. His denial of Me is his statement that I will never repeat His creation like I created him the first time. Yet, the second creation is not more difficult upon Me than the first. His harming Me is his statement that I have a son. Yet, I am One Alone, the Self-Sufficient Whom all creatures need. He Who does not beget children, nor was He born and there is none coequal or comparable unto Him."*

The hadith names two things side by side — denying the resurrection, and ascribing a son to Allah — and answers both by saying who Allah is. And its closing words, that there is "none coequal or comparable unto Him," meet the question of the ayah just before ours: *do you know any one worthy of His name?*

## Allah swears by Himself (68)

**فَوَرَبِّكَ** — "So by your Lord…" Ibn Kathir says simply: the Lord, Blessed be He the Most High, **swears by His Noble Self** that He will definitely gather them. To the sneer of ayah 66, this is the answer given — not a further argument, but an oath.

Who is gathered? Ibn Kathir: all those who worshipped other than Allah, **and their devils as well**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the ayah can be read two ways. First, that on the Day of Judgment every disbeliever will be brought before Allah along with his own devil — the tempter present alongside the tempted. Or, if the address is taken in the general sense to include believers and disbelievers alike, the meaning is that while the disbelievers are gathered with their devils, the believers are gathered at the same time and the same place.

## Brought to their knees — *jithiyyā* (68)

**ثُمَّ لَنُحْضِرَنَّهُمْ حَوْلَ جَهَنَّمَ جِثِيًّا** — "then We shall bring them round Hell, *jithiyyā*."

The early scholars glossed the word in more than one way, and Ibn Kathir preserves the difference rather than flattening it. Al-ʿAwfī related that **Ibn ʿAbbās** said it means *sitting*, comparing it with "And you will see each nation *jāthiyah*" (45:28). **As-Suddī** said it means *standing*, and the same is reported from **Ibn Masʿūd** through Murrah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "fallen on their knees."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the scene out: on the Day of Resurrection everyone — believers and disbelievers, the blessed and the wretched — will be assembled around Hell. Everyone will be seized with awe and terror, and they will all be on their knees. Then the believers and the blessed will be taken across Hell and admitted into Paradise, so that having viewed the extreme suffering of Hell they may all the better enjoy their own state of felicity.

Hold on to that word *jithiyyā*, because it comes back. It is the last word of ayah 72 as well — the wrongdoers are **left** kneeling. Everyone in this passage ends up on their knees; not everyone gets up again.

## Dragged out by rank (69–70)

**ثُمَّ لَنَنزِعَنَّ مِن كُلِّ شِيعَةٍ** — "Then indeed We shall drag out from every *shīʿah*."

**Mujāhid** glossed *shīʿah* as *every nation*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word more fully: it is applied to a particular person or to the followers of a particular faith, and it also means a sect. The sense of the ayah is that the most rebellious from among the different sects of the disbelievers will be picked out — and some commentators, it adds, say that sinners will be committed to Hell in the order of the intensity of their sins: those whose sins are most intense driven in first, then those with less intense sins, and so on.

The description of those picked out is **أَيُّهُمْ أَشَدُّ عَلَى الرَّحْمَٰنِ عِتِيًّا** — "those who were worst in obstinate rebellion **against the Most Gracious**." Of all the divine names, the one the ayah uses here is *ar-Raḥmān*: their rebellion is measured against the Most Gracious.

Ibn Kathir preserves a vivid report from **Ibn Masʿūd**, transmitted by ath-Thawrī from ʿAlī ibn al-Aqmar, from Abū al-Aḥwaṣ: *"The first of them will be bound to the last of them until their number is complete. Then, they will be brought all together. Then, Allah will begin with the greatest of them in crime and continue in succession."* A whole movement of misguidance strung together, no one slipping out at the back — and then a summons that begins at the top.

Ibn Kathir connects this with the mutual recrimination of 7:38–39, where the last of them say of the first, "Our Lord! These misled us, so give them a double torment of the Fire," and the first answer, "You were not better than us, so taste the torment for what you used to earn."

Ayah 70 closes that thought: **ثُمَّ لَنَحْنُ أَعْلَمُ بِالَّذِينَ هُمْ أَوْلَىٰ بِهَا صِلِيًّا** — "Then, verily, We know best those who are most worthy of being burnt therein." Ibn Kathir says Allah here attaches one piece of information to another: He knows best which of His creatures deserve to be burned in the fire of Hell and to remain there forever, and who deserves to have his punishment doubled — as in "He will say: 'For each one there is double (torment), but you know not'" (7:38). The recriminating parties argue over who deserves more; the verdict is not theirs to reach.

## "There is none of you but will come to it" (71)

**وَإِن مِّنكُمْ إِلَّا وَارِدُهَا ۚ كَانَ عَلَىٰ رَبِّكَ حَتْمًا مَّقْضِيًّا**

This is the ayah that stops readers, and the commentators treat it with corresponding care.

**"A decree which must be accomplished."** As-Suddī reported from Murrah, from **Ibn Masʿūd**, that *ḥatman maqḍiyyā* means "an oath that must be fulfilled." **Mujāhid** said *ḥatman* means preordainment, and **Ibn Jurayj** said the same. Either way it is fixed: not a possibility but a settled matter.

**The bridge.** Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Jarīr's report from ʿAbdullāh on this ayah: *"The bridge over Hell is like the sharp edge of a sword. The first group to cross it will pass like a flash of lightning. The second group will pass like the wind. The third group will pass like the fastest horse. The fourth group will pass like the fastest cow. Then, the rest will pass while the angels will be saying, 'O Allah save them, save them.'"* Ibn Kathir notes that this narration has supporting narrations similar to it from the Prophet ﷺ in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs and other collections as well, related by Anas, Abū Saʿīd, Abū Hurayrah, Jābir and other Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all.

**A conversation in Ḥafṣah's house.** Ahmad recorded from Umm Mubashshar, the wife of Zayd ibn Ḥārithah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in the house of Ḥafṣah when he said, *"No one who was present at the battles of Badr and Ḥudaybiyyah (of the Muslims) will enter into the Hellfire."* Ḥafṣah objected: does Allah not say, "There is not one of you but will pass over it"? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ replied by reciting **ثُمَّ نُنَجِّي الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوا** — "Then We shall save those who had *taqwā*."

That exchange is itself a lesson in how to read: ayah 71 is not a standalone sentence. It is completed by ayah 72.

**"Except for an oath that must be fulfilled."** Ibn Kathir places next a hadith in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, reported from az-Zuhrī, from Saʿīd, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"No one of the Muslims who has had three children, who all died, will be touched by the Hellfire, except for an oath that must be fulfilled."* Note the closing phrase — the same "oath that must be fulfilled" by which Ibn Masʿūd glossed *ḥatman maqḍiyyā* in this very ayah.

**What does "coming to it" mean?** Here the scholars differ, and both views are worth having.

- **ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam:** the passing of the Muslims over the Hellfire means their passing over a bridge that is over it; but the passing of the idolaters over the Hellfire refers to their admission to the Fire. One word, two utterly different experiences.
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān:** everybody, believer or disbeliever, will go *across* Hell — this does not mean they would go to stay in it. And even if the word means "entry," the pious believers on entry will feel no discomfort, because its fires will cool down and do them no harm. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates on the authority of Abū Sumayya that the Prophet ﷺ once said that everybody, pious man or sinner, will initially enter Hell, but that for the pious believers the fire will cool down just as the fire of Namrūd cooled down when Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) was cast into it, and thereafter the believers will be taken to Paradise. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this view is confirmed by the next sentence, "Then We shall save those who had taqwā," and reports a similar view from **Ibn ʿAbbās**: even if *wurūd* is taken to mean *dukhūl* (entry), *dukhūl* here is interpreted as synonymous with *ʿubūr* (going across) — so there is no contradiction in the meaning of the word.

## "Then We shall save those who had taqwā" (72)

Ibn Kathir sets out the sequence. When all of the creatures have passed over the Hellfire — and those disbelievers and disobedient people destined to fall into it because of their disobedience have fallen — Allah will save the believers and the righteous from it **because of their deeds**. Their passing over the bridge, and their speed, will be based upon the deeds they did in this life. That is why the report above has some crossing like a flash of lightning, and the rest passing while the angels say, "O Allah save them, save them."

Then comes intercession. The believers who performed major sins will be allowed intercession: the angels, the Prophets and the believers will all intercede. A large number of the sinners will be allowed to come out of Hell, the fire having devoured much of their bodies **except the places of prostration on their faces**. Their removal will be due to the faith in their hearts, and the order will follow its weight: first the one with the weight of a dīnār of faith in his heart, then whoever has the next least amount after him, and so forth, until the one with the tiniest hint of faith, equal to the weight of an atom. Then Allah will take out of the Fire whoever said *lā ilāha illa Allāh* even one day of his entire life, even if he never performed any good deed. After that, no one will remain in the Hellfire except those upon whom it is obligatory to remain there forever. Ibn Kathir states that this has been reported in many authentic hadiths from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

And then the last clause: **وَنَذَرُ الظَّالِمِينَ فِيهَا جِثِيًّا** — "And We shall leave the wrongdoers in it, kneeling." They are left in the posture everyone was in at ayah 68, while everyone else is taken across and out of it.

## Living it

**The proof offered to the doubter is his own beginning.** Ibn Kathir's whole answer is the first creation: you were nothing, and here you are. And by 30:27 the second creation is the easier of the two — so the astonishment is aimed at the wrong end.

**Hold both ayat together.** Ḥafṣah heard glad tidings and immediately tested them against the Book — and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ met her objection by reciting the next words. Fear (ayah 71) without ayah 72 is despair; comfort without ayah 71 is complacency. The passage refuses to be quoted in halves.

**Your deeds are your speed.** Ibn Kathir is explicit that the passing over the bridge, and the speed of it, will be based upon the deeds a person did in this life. Nothing else in this passage is in our hands; that is.

**Do not sort people into the Fire.** Ayah 70 reserves that knowledge — who is *most worthy* of burning, who remains forever, whose punishment is doubled — to Allah alone. The parties in 7:38–39 spend their time assigning blame to each other and are told, "you know not."

**Never write anyone off, and never presume for yourself.** Ibn Kathir's account ends with people leaving the Fire for an atom's weight of faith, or a single day's *lā ilāha illa Allāh*. That is a reason to keep hoping for people. But it is the end of a very long queue, after the fire has devoured much of the body; nobody reading it honestly would aim for that place in the line.

**Note who is being defied.** Ayah 69 calls them worst in obstinate rebellion *against the Most Gracious* — the rebellion is measured against the One who is *ar-Raḥmān*.

passages.title: The boast of rank and assembly, answered by ruins
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** The leaders of Mecca hear the clear signs of Allah recited to them, turn away, and answer with a boast about their dwellings and their well-attended assemblies — as though comfort settled the argument. These four ayat hold together as one exchange: ayah 73 records the boast, ayah 74 answers it with destroyed generations, ayah 75 explains why such people are still standing at all, and ayah 76 names the only increase and the only wealth that survive.

## The boast (ayah 73)

Ibn Kathir explains that when the clear, evident ayat of Allah are recited to the disbelievers, "they reject them and turn away." Then they speak about the believers, "boasting to them and arguing that their false religion is correct": *"Which of the two groups has the best dwellings and the finest Nadiyyan?"*

Two Arabic words carry the whole taunt:

- **مَقَام (maqām)** — rendered in the translation as *dwellings*. Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase as "the best houses, with the loftiest levels." Al-A'mash reported from Abu Zibyan from Ibn 'Abbas: "Position [Maqam] means home." Al-'Awfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "Position [Maqam] means dwelling," together with "the blessing and happiness that they were living in."
- **نَدِيّ (nadiyy)** — Ibn Kathir: "meeting rooms for men to gather and discuss matters," so the boast means "that their meeting rooms are full of more people who come to attend." In the report al-'Awfi relates from Ibn 'Abbas, *nadī* is "the places of gathering and meeting where they used to congregate," and the same report cites Allah's words about the people of Lut, *"And practice Al-Munkar (evil deeds) in your meeting places [Nadiyakum]"* (29:29), concluding: "The Arabs call a place of gathering a Nadi."

So the claim is property and popularity: better addresses, fuller rooms. Ibn Kathir puts their unspoken argument in one sentence: *"How can we be upon falsehood while we are in this manner of successful living?"*

**Who they were sneering at.** Ibn Kathir adds a detail that puts a face on the scene: the believers being measured against them were "those who were concealed in the house of Al-Arqam bin Abi Al-Arqam and its likes from the other houses." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the same contrast: the disbelievers "were very rich and possessed material wealth in great abundance," with "their retinues, their followers, friends and supporters," while "the believers were poor and lacking in worldly assets." By the two yardsticks the Meccans chose, the Muslims lost on both counts — which was exactly the point of the jibe.

**An argument as old as prophethood.** Ibn Kathir gathers the parallels. The disbelievers say of the believers, *"Had it been a good thing, they (the weak and the poor) would not have preceded us thereto"* (46:11). Nuh's people said, *"Shall we believe in you, when the weakest (of the people) follow you?"* (26:111). And Allah says, *"Thus We have tried some of them with others, that they might say: Is it these (poor believers) whom Allah has favored among us? Does not Allah know best those who are grateful?"* (6:53). Sneering at the poor for reaching the truth first is not a Meccan invention; it is the standard reflex of rejection.

## Answered by destroyed generations (ayah 74)

"This is why Allah refuted their doubts," says Ibn Kathir — and notice how the refutation works. Allah does not deny that they are comfortable. He grants the claim and then doubles it: *"And how many a generation have We destroyed before them, who were better in wealth, goods and outward appearance."* Ibn Kathir reads the opening as, "How many nations and generations did We destroy of those who denied (this message) due to their disbelief?" and the second half as meaning "they were better than these present people in wealth, possessions, looks and appearance."

The two words repay attention. **أَثَاث (athāth)** is rendered *wealth, goods*, which Ibn 'Abbas glosses as "material possessions"; **رِئْي (ri'ya)** is rendered *outward appearance*, which Ibn 'Abbas explains as "how they look physically" — the impression a people make on the eye. Both boasts are conceded and then set against a fact the boasters could not answer: the people who scored higher on exactly these measures are the ones Allah destroyed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it flatly: "History is replete with instances where prosperous communities and rich nations crumbled to dust and vanished without leaving a trace."

Al-'Awfi's report from Ibn 'Abbas draws the comparison with Fir'awn's people, of whom Allah said after destroying them, *"How many gardens and springs that they left behind, and green crops and honored places [Maqam]"* (44:25–26) — the very word the Meccans were using for their own boast, applied by Allah to what a ruined people left behind. Ibn 'Abbas concludes: "position [Maqam] refers to their dwellings and splendid bounties, and Nadi is the places of gathering and meeting where they used to congregate."

## Why wealth is such a persuasive liar

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the psychology behind ayah 73. "The infidels never relaxed their efforts to confuse and perplex the believers." Then comes the diagnosis: "it is a common experience that material wealth turns people's heads and makes them unduly proud and arrogant, so that even the sensible and wise among them are led to believe that their prosperity and affluence is the reward of their personal merit and effort, and will last forever."

Two false conclusions sit inside that sentence — *I earned this* and *this will last* — and the history Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to breaks both at once. Yet, it adds, "these instances of Divine wrath hold no lesson for them and fail to turn them from their erroneous ways."

Against that, the commentary describes those who are immune to the disease: people who, following the teachings of the Qur'an, "do not regard wealth and worldly honors as the result of their own effort and merit, but as Allah Ta'ala's bounty to be held as a trust from Him and to be expended according to His command." Knowing the gift will not last forever, "the prospect of their abatement or even their total loss does not cause them any concern." These, it says, "are the people who are safe from the mischief resulting from wealth and material abundance to which the infidels are exposed." Wealth is not the problem; the reading of wealth is. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names as examples the Prophets Sulayman and Dawud (peace be upon them), many of the followers of the Prophet ﷺ, and a multitude among the pious believers — people of means whose means never owned them.

The conclusion is stated plainly: "transient material prosperity cannot be regarded as a token of His goodwill nor as a symbol of their own merit, because it often happens that foolish and undeserving people are loaded with wealth while wise and learned persons spend their lives in poverty."

## Respite is not approval (ayah 75)

Ibn Kathir heads his comment on this ayah: **"The Rebellious Person is given Respite but He is not forgotten."**

*"Say"* — Ibn Kathir: "O Muhammad, say to these people who are associating partners with their Lord, while claiming to follow the truth, that they are really following falsehood." What follows is put in deliberately even-handed terms: *"whoever is in error"* means, in Ibn Kathir's words, "be they from us or from you." The Prophet ﷺ is told to state a rule that applies to whichever side is actually astray — a rule that will sort the two parties by itself.

The one who grants the extension is named in the ayah as **al-Raḥmān**, rendered here "the Most Gracious," and in Ibn Kathir's own paraphrase "the Most Beneficent": *"the Most Gracious will extend [circumstances] for him"* means "that the Most Beneficent will give him respite in that which he is in, until he meets his Lord and his appointed time will have arrived." The extra years a wrongdoer enjoys are not an oversight and not a verdict in his favour — as Ibn Kathir's heading says, he is given respite, but he is not forgotten.

The extension has an end written into it: *"until, when they see that which they were promised, either the torment"* — which, says Ibn Kathir, "will strike him" — *"or the Hour"* — "that will come suddenly." At that moment, *"they will come to know who is worst in position (makān), and who is weaker in forces (jund)."*

Read that closing line against the boast of ayah 73 and the structure snaps into place. Ibn Kathir says explicitly: "This is in refutation of their argument about their nice dwellings and splendid places of gathering." They said *best in maqām* — Allah answers *worst in makān*. They said *finest in nadiyy*, our rooms are fuller — Allah answers *weaker in jund*, weaker in forces. Both claims are answered in their own vocabulary, simply relocated to the day that decides them.

Ibn Kathir then reads ayah 75 as "a challenge against the idolators who claim that they were following guidance in what they were doing," and sets it beside two others in the Qur'an. To the Jews: *"O you Jews! If you pretend that you are friends of Allah, to the exclusion of (all) other people, then long for death if you are truthful"* (62:6) — meaning, he explains, "Supplicate for death to come to those who are following falsehood among us if you truly claim to be upon the truth. If you are true, then this supplication will not harm you." He notes: "But they refused to do so," and that an extensive discussion of this has already preceded in Surat al-Baqarah. And to the Christians who persisted in the claim that 'Isa was the son of Allah — after Allah had set out His arguments and proofs "that he was merely a creature like Adam" — came the invitation to mutual imprecation: *"Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves - then we pray and invoke (sincerely) the curse of Allah upon those who lie"* (3:61). "However, they (the Christians) also retreated from this challenge." A claim that will not stand being tested has already told you what it is worth.

## The other increase (ayah 76)

Ibn Kathir catches the hinge between the two ayat: "After Allah mentions the extended time and respite that is allowed to those who are in misguidance, increasing them in misguidance, He informs of the increase in guidance of those who are rightly guided." Two ledgers, both growing: the misguided are given more time and increase in misguidance; the guided are increased in guidance. Ibn Kathir cites as a parallel, *"And whenever there comes down a Surah, some of them say: Which of you has had his faith increased by it?"* (9:124).

**"And the righteous good deeds that last" (al-bāqiyāt al-ṣāliḥāt).** Ibn Kathir notes that the explanation of this phrase "has already preceded in Surat Al-Kahf, along with a lengthy discussion concerning it," and does not repeat it here. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise says the words "have been interpreted differently by different scholars," and gives its own preference: "The more plausible interpretation, however, is that the words refer to submission to the commands of Allah and to good deeds, the benefits of which are everlasting." The commentators do not confine the phrase to one narrow list; on this reading, its defining feature is that the benefit does not stop.

*"They are better with your Lord for reward"* — Ibn Kathir: "the recompense and reward." *"And better for resort (maraddan)"* — Ibn Kathir: "the final outcome, the result for its doer"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: *maraddan* "means consequences, and the sense of this verse is that good deeds alone are the real wealth whose reward is great and whose result is eternal peace."

There is a quiet completion here. The passage opened with men bragging about their dwellings and their assemblies; it closes on what a person returns to, and on the deeds that are still there when he arrives.

## Living it

- **Do not read prosperity as a verdict.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that worldly abundance is neither "a token of His goodwill nor as a symbol of their own merit." The generations Allah destroyed in ayah 74 were "better in wealth, goods and outward appearance" than the men who were boasting.
- **Do not read smallness as a verdict either.** The believers in this passage were the ones "concealed in the house of Al-Arqam bin Abi Al-Arqam and its likes from the other houses," poor and lacking in worldly assets. That said nothing about the truth they carried.
- **Hold what you have as a trust.** The safe posture Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes is to treat wealth and honour as Allah's bounty, "held as a trust from Him and to be expended according to His command," with no alarm at the thought of losing it.
- **Do not mistake a long run for a clean record.** Ibn Kathir's heading is the whole warning: the rebellious person is given respite, but he is not forgotten.
- **Invest where the return does not expire.** *Al-bāqiyāt al-ṣāliḥāt* — on Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's preferred reading, submission to Allah's commands and deeds whose benefits are everlasting — are "the real wealth whose reward is great and whose result is eternal peace."

passages.title: The scoffer who claims wealth in the Hereafter
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Four ayat that take apart a single sneer. A Makkan opponent of the Prophet ﷺ told a Muslim who was owed money that even resurrection would not disturb his comfort — he would have wealth and children in the next life too, and could settle the debt there. Ayah 77 quotes the boast, ayah 78 asks him where he obtained such information, ayah 79 tells him what Allah will do with the words themselves, and ayah 80 tells him what he will actually arrive with. The unity of the passage is that one sentence, followed from the mouth that spoke it to the Day it is answered.

## The scene behind the words

Ibn Kathir grounds these ayat in a report of Imam Ahmad from Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, may Allah be pleased with him. Khabbab said that he was a blacksmith and that al-'As ibn Wa'il owed him a debt. He went to collect it. Al-'As swore he would not pay until Khabbab disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ. Khabbab swore in return that he would not disbelieve in Muhammad ﷺ until al-'As died and was resurrected. Al-'As then said that if he did die and was raised, and Khabbab came to him, he would also have abundance of wealth and children there, and would repay him then. Ibn Kathir says Allah then revealed these ayat, from "Have you seen him who disbelieved in Our Ayat" to "and he shall come to Us alone."

He adds that the report "was also recorded by the two compilers of the Sahihs and other collections as well," and that in the wording of al-Bukhari, Khabbab says he was a blacksmith in Makkah who had made a sword for al-'As ibn Wa'il and went to collect his pay. Maʿarif ul Qurʼan relates the same episode — citing Qurtubi, and saying that Bukhari and Muslim relate it — in a slightly different form: that Khabbab had lent al-'As some money, and that when pressed for repayment al-'As demanded he dissociate himself from the Prophet ﷺ, then scoffed, "What? Will I be brought to life again after I am dead?" — adding that even then he would have his wealth and his children.

Notice the shape of the exchange, because the ayat answer every part of it.

**A debt used as leverage over a man's faith.** Al-'As did not argue theology. He simply held back money a working man had earned and named a price: renounce Muhammad ﷺ and you get paid.

**Khabbab's answer is the answer of certainty.** "Not until you die and are resurrected" is not a delay tactic; it is a man saying that the Resurrection is so certain to him that he will happily set his appointment by it.

**And al-'As turns the Resurrection into a joke.** He picks up Khabbab's own words and mocks them: fine, I will be raised — and I will have wealth and children there too. The sarcasm carries an assumption: a man so well supplied in this world cannot imagine any world in which he is not.

This is why Ibn Kathir titles the section a refutation of "the Disbelievers Who claim that They will be given Wealth and Children in the Hereafter." The ayat begin with one man's remark but settle a whole attitude.

## Ayah 77: the boast, quoted back at him

**"Have you seen…"** The address is to the Prophet ﷺ — and through him, to everyone listening. It is the tone of someone being invited to look at something astonishing: *look at this man, look at what he just said.*

**"the one who rejects Our revelations."** He is not described as a debtor or a chief. He is defined by what he did with the ayat of Allah. Everything else in the passage follows from that one relationship.

**"I shall certainly be given wealth and children."** Ibn Kathir puts the absurdity precisely. Speaking of the man who says this — meaning, he explains, on the Day of Resurrection — he asks: "Does he know what he will have in the Hereafter, to such an extent that he can swear to it?" That is the exact size of the claim. Not a hope, not a guess about the unseen, but a statement a man would stake an oath on. He denies Allah's signs, and then announces what Allah will hand him.

**Wealth and children.** Hold on to these two, because ayah 80 comes back for exactly them.

## Ayah 78: two doors, and both are shut

Ayah 78 does not shout him down. It asks a question — and it is a question with exactly two possible answers, neither of which is available to him.

**"Has he looked into the unseen?"** Maʿarif ul Qurʼan renders it vividly: "Has he peeped in the unseen?" — as though a man could put his eye to a crack in the wall of the future and see his own account balance on the Day of Judgement. Ibn Kathir says this is a rejection of the person who says "I shall certainly be given wealth and children," meaning on the Day of Resurrection. Maʿarif adds the obvious: "It is obvious that nothing of this kind has happened. Then why has he considered it as a surety?"

**"or has he taken a covenant from the Most Gracious?"** The second door. Ibn Kathir explains the covenant (*'ahd*) here as "an agreement," and notes that this explanation is mentioned in Sahih Al-Bukhari. So the question is, as he puts it: "Or has he received a promise from Allah that he will be given these things?" Maʿarif asks the same — has he entered into a covenant with Allah and obtained a promise from Him for his wealth and his children?

Between them these two questions close off every route to such a claim. They assume that what awaits a person after death is *al-ghayb*, the unseen — not something a man can inspect for himself. So the only two ways to know it would be the two the ayah names: Allah shows him, or Allah promises him. Al-'As had neither. He had only a hunch dressed as a certainty.

There is a quiet irony here worth pausing on. The man mocking revelation is making a confident statement about the unseen — the very thing he could only know if Allah had shown him or promised him. He rejects the messenger and then helps himself to the messenger's subject matter.

**Why this name for Allah?** The name in the second question is *ar-Rahman* — rendered "the Most Gracious" in the translation of Ibn Kathir before us, and by Maʿarif ul Qurʼan as "The Rahman (All-Merciful)." Even in a passage of rebuke, the name under which such a covenant would have been made is the name of mercy. But note what the ayah does with it: mercy is real, and it is given through Allah's own promise — not assumed by a man who has rejected His signs.

## Ayah 79: "Not at all"

**كَلَّا — "Nay," "Not at all."** Ibn Kathir pauses on this small word. In the translation before us his comment reads: "This is a participle that opposes what came before it and gives emphasis to what follows it." So it works in two directions at once. It slams the door on the boast, and it drives home the sentence that answers it.

**"We certainly record whatever he claims."** Ibn Kathir says what is recorded is not merely the sentence he uttered, but "what he is seeking, and his idea that he has given himself about what he hopes for, and his disbelief in Allah the Most Great." That is a striking expansion. The record takes in three layers: the words, the wish behind the words, and the rejection of Allah underneath them both. He treated the remark as a throwaway line to a creditor. It went into a book.

**"and We shall increase his torment."** Ibn Kathir: "This is referring to what will happen in the abode of the Hereafter, because of his saying his disbelief in Allah in this life."

Look at what the answer does with his own vocabulary. He was counting on *more* — more wealth, more children, in the next world. He will be given more: more punishment. The increase he expected arrives, in the one currency he never considered.

## Ayah 80: the inheritance and the arrival

**"And We will inherit what he boasts of."** Ibn Kathir says this means his wealth and children: "We will take all of this from him, in opposition to his claim that he will be given more wealth and children in the Hereafter than he had in this life. To the contrary, in the Hereafter that which he had in this life will be taken from him."

Feel the word *inherit*. An heir takes possession of what a person leaves behind when he is gone; property passes out of the hands of the one who thought he owned it. Maʿarif ul Qurʼan states the point plainly: it is foolish of him to talk about retaining his wealth and children in the Hereafter, because he will have to leave behind even the things he possesses in this world — his wealth and his children will all revert to Allah.

So the boast is not merely denied a bonus; it is reversed at the root. He hoped for an increase on his current holdings. He will not even keep the holdings.

**"and he shall come to Us alone."** Ibn Kathir's gloss on this is four words long and devastating: "without wealth or children." He named two things in ayah 77; ayah 80 removes exactly those two. Maʿarif ul Qurʼan says the same: on the Day of Judgement he will appear in Allah's presence without his wealth and his children.

The passage therefore ends with a picture rather than an argument. A man who could not conceive of himself except as wealthy and surrounded, standing there as nothing but himself — while the words he threw away that day are, by ayah 79, still on record.

## What this asks of us

**Do not let comfort become evidence.** What the ayat challenge in al-'As is not a rival theology; it is a confidence with nothing behind it. They do not debate him. They ask him where he got his information.

**Speak about the unseen only from revelation.** Ayah 78 names the only two grounds anyone could have for a claim about what comes after death: disclosure from Allah, or a promise from Him. Anything else — intuition, confidence, the feeling that things will work out — is exactly what this ayah asks about and finds empty.

**Your words are being written.** Ayah 79 records not only the remark, but the wish and the disbelief inside it. That is worth remembering about the things we say lightly, especially things said about Allah, His signs, or the Day of Judgement.

**Nothing you own is owned.** Ayah 80 speaks of Allah inheriting a living man's wealth and children, and Maʿarif ul Qurʼan spells out why that is not a threat but a fact: even what he has in this world he must leave behind, and it reverts to Allah.

**And take heart from Khabbab.** He was the poor man in that room, owed money, offered a straightforward way out: say one sentence against the Prophet ﷺ and get paid. He refused — and, as Ibn Kathir reports it, Allah then revealed these ayat, quoting his opponent's boast and settling it forever. The powerful man's sentence survives only inside the revelation that refutes it; the blacksmith's refusal is remembered as the occasion on which these ayat came down.

passages.title: False gods will disown their worshippers
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** These four ayat take apart the whole logic of worshipping anything besides Allah. People take other gods hoping for honour and might; on the Day of Judgement those very gods will deny their worship and turn on them (81–82). Meanwhile the devils are pushing them onward in this life (83). And to the Prophet ﷺ, watching all this, Allah says: make no haste — We are counting (84). What holds the unit together is a single movement from the false hope, to its reversal, to the hidden pressure driving it, to the calm certainty that the account is already being kept.

The passage follows on from the man of 19:80. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it there, it was foolish of him to talk about retaining his wealth and children in the Hereafter, because he will have to leave behind even the things he possesses in this world, and his wealth and children will all revert to Allah — and, in the words of the ayah, "And he will come to Us all alone," appearing on the Day of Judgement without his wealth and without his children. Ayah 81 now widens the lens from one man to a whole way of life built on the same mistake.

## Ayah 81 — the bargain that looked so sensible

**"They have taken other gods, instead of Allah, seeking strength."** Ibn Kathir renders the ayah, "And they have taken gods besides Allah, that they might give them honor, power and glory," and reads the motive plainly: Allah is informing us about the disbelievers who associate partners with their Lord, that they have taken these gods besides Allah "so that these gods may be a source of honor and might for them."

Notice what the ayah says the idols were *for*. Ibn Kathir spells out the thinking behind it: "They think that these gods give them power and make them victorious." Seen from inside, the calculation had its own logic. They wanted honour, might and victory. They wanted a patron in the unseen so that they would not be alone and would not lose.

## Ayah 82 — "But no!" and the reversal

**"Nay, but they will deny their worship of them, and will become their adversaries."** The ayah opens with a flat refusal — the translation renders it "But no!", Ibn Kathir "Nay." Ibn Kathir's summary of the turn is exact: "the matter is not as they claim, and it will not be as they hope."

Then comes the sentence they never imagined: they will deny their worship. Ibn Kathir specifies the timing — this happens "on the Day of Judgement." As-Suddi glosses what is denied: "This means their worshipping of the idols." The very beings on whom they staked their honour disown the whole transaction.

And more than disowned: **"and will become their adversaries."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān translates the phrase, "And they will be just the opposite for them." Ibn Kathir explains that they will be foes "in a state other than what they think about these gods," that is, "contrary to what they hoped for from these gods." Two early authorities sharpen it: As-Suddi said it means, "They will be in severe opposition and argument"; Ad-Dahhak said simply, "This means enemies." So the reversal is total. What was sought as honour, power and glory arrives as adversaries — severe opposition and argument from the very quarter they expected backing.

Ibn Kathir brings a parallel from Sūrat al-Aḥqāf that says the same thing twice over: "And who is more astray than one who calls upon, besides Allah, such as will not answer him till the Day of Resurrection, and who are (even) unaware of their calls to them? And when mankind are gathered, they will become their enemies and will deny their worshipping" (46:5–6). Two failures are stacked in those lines. In this life the ones called upon are *unaware* of the calls addressed to them. In the next life they turn up as enemies.

**What the idols will say.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the scene: the idols and false gods whom the infidels worshipped in the hope of winning their help will turn against them on the Day of Judgement. Allah will grant them speech, and they will call on Allah to finish these sinners — because they turned away from Him and made the idols the objects of their worship. Sit with that for a moment. The thing you served does not merely abandon you; it asks for your ruin, and it does so on the ground that your worship was a turning away from Allah. Every hope of winning their help collapses in that one sentence.

## Ayah 83 — the pressure you cannot see

**"See you not that We have sent the Shayatin against the disbelievers to push them to do evil."** That is Ibn Kathir's rendering; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the closing phrase, "Inciting them with all their incitements." Having shown the end of the road, the passage now shows what is driving the traffic along it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a small lesson in Arabic here. The words ḥaḍḍ, fazz, azz and hazz are synonymous, differing only in shade or degree, and mean to urge, incite, instigate. Among them, **azz** means "to apply strong pressure, to persuade somebody to do something." And Maʿārif describes the method precisely: the devils instigate the unbelievers to persist in their evil ways "by presenting before their eyes the benefits and hiding from them the wickedness of their evil deeds." That is the technique of temptation in one line — magnify the payoff, keep the cost off-screen.

Ibn Kathir titles this section "The Power of the Devils over the Disbelievers," and the early commentators he quotes describe the effect from different angles, which together give a full picture:

- **Ibn ʿAbbas** (reported by ʿAli bin Abi Talhah): "They will lead them astray with temptation."
- **Ibn ʿAbbas** (reported by al-ʿAwfi): "They will incite them against Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions." — the pressure was not only inward toward sin; it was outward into hostility against the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions.
- **Qatadah**: "They will harass them and disturb them until they disobey Allah." Wearing a person down until obedience finally gives way.
- **ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd** connects it to another ayah: "And whosoever turns away blindly from the remembrance of the Most Gracious, We appoint for him a Shaytan to be a companion for him" (43:36).

That last citation repays attention, because of the order inside it: the turning away comes first in the sentence, and the appointed companion follows. Read alongside our ayah — where those pushed are named as the disbelievers — it describes a closing in on someone who has already turned away.

**"See you not"** is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ; the translation makes the address explicit, "Do you ˹O Prophet˺ not see." It asks him to recognise something that the situation on the ground does not show on its face.

## Ayah 84 — make no haste; We are counting

**"So make no haste against them; We only count out to them a (limited) number."** Ibn Kathir reads it as spoken directly to the Prophet ﷺ: "Do not be hasty with the punishment that is going to befall them, O Muhammad."

Then the reason — and it is not a denial that judgement is coming, but the opposite. "We only count out to them a number" means, in Ibn Kathir's words, "We are only delaying them for a fixed appointment whose time is numbered. They are destined for that and there is no escaping the torment of Allah and His exemplary punishment." As-Suddi breaks the counting down: it "means years, months, days and hours."

Ibn Kathir then gathers a cluster of ayat that all say the same thing — respite is not neglect:

- "And consider not that Allah is unaware of that which the wrongdoers do" (14:42).
- "So give a respite to the disbelievers; deal gently with them for a while" (86:17).
- "We postpone the punishment only so that they may increase in sinfulness" (3:178).
- "We let them enjoy for a little while, then in the end We shall oblige them to (enter) a great torment" (31:24).
- "Say: 'Enjoy! But certainly, your destination is the (Hell) Fire'" (14:30).

Read together, they overturn the instinct that delay means escape.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same reading and then turns the counting toward the reader. The meaning, it says, is: "Do not be impatient about their punishment because it is going to befall upon them in any case - and very soon. We have allowed them a fixed term in this world and that term is about to end. Then will come their retribution." And on the phrase *naʿuddu lahum*: "We are counting for them, i.e. they do not have control on anything. Their days are numbered and We keep a count of every moment of their life and everything they do."

**A scene worth remembering.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that Ma'mun Rashid once read Sūrah Maryam, and on reaching this ayah he asked Ibn Simak, one of the Islamic scholars sitting in that gathering with him, to say something about it. Ibn Simak's reply was that when our breaths are numbered and their number cannot be enhanced, they will soon come to an end. Maʿārif cites a line of poetry to the same effect: the breaths of your life are counted, and with every passing breath your life gets reduced to that extent. It adds, from Qurtubi, that it is said one breathes twenty-four thousand times during a span of twenty-four hours. And a second stanza, cited from Ruh, in the same vein: how can one be so engrossed and relaxed with worldly pleasures, while his words and his breaths are being counted?
