That is the turn that makes this ayah personal. "We are counting" was first said about those whose term is running out. Ibn Simak heard it as being about himself.

## Living it

**Check what you are quietly relying on for honour and might.** Ayah 81, as Ibn Kathir reads it, names the motive behind idolatry: people took these gods so that they might be a source of honour and might for them, believing they give power and make victorious. Very few people today keep a stone idol. But the question the ayah asks still lands: what is it that you believe is really making you strong and secure? Whatever that is, ayah 82 says the same thing about all of it — on the Day it will not stand where you expected it to stand.

**Assume the pressure is real, and name it.** Ayah 83 tells us that persistence in wrong is pushed, not merely chosen — with the benefits presented before the eyes and the wickedness of the deed hidden, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes. Being able to recognise that pattern in the moment ("I am being shown only the upside of this") is itself a defence. And the ayah ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd cites points to where the danger begins: turning away blindly from the remembrance of the Most Gracious.

**Let go of the demand for immediate justice.** Ayah 84 is a mercy to anyone watching wrong go unanswered. Ibn Kathir's cluster of ayat makes the point from every side: Allah is not unaware of what the wrongdoers do, the respite is measured, and there is no escaping His punishment. The appointment is fixed and its time is numbered.

**And hear the counting as being about you too.** That is Ibn Simak's insight, and it is the gentlest and most searching thing in the passage. The same precision that numbers their days numbers ours.

passages.title: The righteous honoured, the wicked driven to Hell
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These three ayat show the end of the two roads the sūrah has been laying side by side: the people of taqwā carried to the Most Merciful as an honoured delegation (85), the criminals driven to Hell parched and herded (86), and then the question of who, in that moment, can plead for anyone at all (87). Ibn Kathir treats all three together under one heading: *the condition of the righteous and the criminals on the Day of Resurrection*. What holds them as a unit is a single scene with two processions moving in opposite directions, and a closing note on the one thing that could change a person's place in it — a covenant taken with Allah.

## Who the two groups are

Ibn Kathir does not leave *al-muttaqīn* (rendered "those with taqwā") as a vague label. He describes them as Allah's righteous friends "who feared Him in the life of this world. They followed His Messengers and believed in what the Messengers told them. They obeyed them in what they commanded them and abstained from that which they prohibited." So taqwā here is not a mood; it is measured against the Messengers — believing them, obeying what they brought, staying away from what they forbade.

The other party, *al-mujrimīn* (the criminals), he defines just as concretely: those "who denied the Messengers and opposed them." The two groups are separated by their response to the same call.

## Ayah 85: *wafd* — arriving as a delegation

Everything in ayah 85 turns on one word. A **wafd**, Ibn Kathir explains, "is a group that arrives while riding, and from it comes the word *wufūd* (arriving)." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the social colour: the word "applies to those who are received by rulers and princes with respect and honour." And Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah transmits from him, glossed the word in a single syllable: **"Riding."**

Three things come with that image, and none of them is decorative:

- **They ride.** Ibn Kathir says they will come "riding upon noble steeds of light from the riding animals of the Hereafter."
- **They arrive with standing.** On Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's definition, a *wafd* is precisely the sort of party that rulers receive "with respect and honour" — not a crowd shuffling in, but guests whose arrival is an occasion.
- **They are expected.** Ibn Kathir names the One who receives them: they will arrive "before the Best Receiver of delegations, at the abode of His honour and pleasure." A delegation implies a host who has arranged the welcome.

Notice the destination the ayah itself names: they are gathered **ilā al-Raḥmān** — *to the Most Merciful*. And the verb is *naḥshuru*, "We gather" — the gathering is done by Allah Himself.

## Ayah 86: *wird* — driven, thirsty

Ayah 86 flips every element. The verb changes to *nasūqu*, "We drive" — Ibn Kathir says the criminals "will be driven violently to the Hellfire." The rendering of the ayah given here is "drive the wicked to Hell like a thirsty herd": not led with honour, but driven.

And the word that answers *wafd* is **wird**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the root sense: "*wird* means to go towards water, and since only a thirsty man or animal goes towards water, this word has been translated to denote a thirsty person." Ibn Kathir reports the same reading — "parched and thirsting for drink" — and notes it was the position of ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah "and many others."

So both words describe an arrival, and that is the sting of the pairing. One party arrives as guests received in honour; the other is driven forward like a thirsty herd going down to water — except that what they are driven to is Jahannam.

## The mounts of the believers

On what exactly the delegation rides, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records two explanations without deciding between them:

1. **Their worldly mounts.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says: "According to some sayings of the Holy Prophet ﷺ he said, 'These men will ride on their mounts which they used in their worldly life.'" This is worth holding lightly. The commentary names no collection for it, and no chain of narration is given, so it cannot be weighed the way a sourced report can — it is passed on here only as the commentary itself states it, and nothing in what follows depends on it.
2. **Their deeds, given a form.** "Some say that their own virtuous deeds will take the shape of their mounts."

For that second view, Ibn Kathir preserves a striking narration with its transmission named: Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from ʿAmr bin Qays al-Mulāʾī, from Ibn Marzūq, that when the believer comes out of his grave he meets the most handsome form he has ever seen, carrying the nicest fragrance. He asks, "Who are you?" It replies, "You do not know me?" He says, "No — but Allah has made you sweet smelling with a handsome face." It answers: **"I am your righteous deeds. This is how you used to beautify and apply fragrance to your deeds in the worldly life. I was riding upon you in the entire length of your worldly life, so will you not ride upon me now?"** And the believer mounts it.

This is the saying of Ibn Marzūq as Ibn Kathir cites it — not a statement attributed to the Prophet ﷺ. But sit with its logic, which is the narration's own: in this life you carry your deeds; on that Day the weight reverses, and what you carried carries you. And the fragrance is not applied on the Day itself. In the narration's words, it is how "you used to beautify and apply fragrance to your deeds in the worldly life."

## A question placed inside the scene

At exactly this point — the two processions in view — Ibn Kathir sets a verse from earlier in the sūrah. "Here it will be said," he writes, and then quotes: *"Which of the two groups is best in Maqām (position) and the finest Nadiyyan (meeting place)?"* (19:73)

He adds no comment of his own to it. He simply places the question in the scene and leaves it there, beside the sight of who rides and who is driven.

## Ayah 87: intercession is not held in anyone's hand

Ibn Kathir's rendering of the ayah is: *"None shall have the power of intercession, but such a one as has received permission (or promise) from the Most Gracious."* The translation given with the ayah puts it: *"None will have the right to intercede, except those who have..."* Power, right — either way, the negation is about possession. On that Day intercession is not something a person has in hand to spend.

Ibn Kathir reads the negation as being about the criminals of ayah 86: "There will be no one who can intercede for them like the believers who intercede for each other." That phrasing quietly affirms the other side of it — that the believers *do* intercede for one another. He then lets the criminals speak in their own words from another sūrah: *"Now we have no intercessors, nor a close friend"* (26:100–101). No one to plead for them, and no close friend either.

## The exception

The ayah then says: *"except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful."* Ibn Kathir calls this **"a separate exclusion,"** and his own paraphrase shows what he takes that to mean: *"But those who have taken a covenant with the Most Beneficent."* Read that way, the ayah is not saying that some criminals will turn out to hold intercession after all; it turns to a different set of people altogether — those who took a covenant with the Most Merciful.

**What is that covenant?** Ibn Kathir: it "is the testimony that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah, and upholding of its rights and implications." Ibn ʿAbbās, again through ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah, unpacks it into three strands: "the testimony that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah, that the person accepts that all power and strength belong to Allah, and he only places his hope with Allah alone."

Read those slowly, because together they describe a whole inner life: the tongue affirms tawḥīd (that Allah alone is worshipped); the self stops claiming any power of its own; the heart places its hope in Allah alone. And Ibn Kathir's phrase "upholding of its rights and implications" makes clear this is not a formula recited once. A covenant is kept.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the scholars' views on *ʿahd* (covenant): Ibn ʿAbbās said it means "a declaration of firm belief in the Unity of Allah," while "others say that *ʿahd* means committing the Qurʼān to memory." Its own summary, citing Rūḥ, is: "only those people will have the permission to intercede with Allah who stand firm by their covenant to adhere to the true faith."

That summary marks a real difference of angle between the two commentaries. **Ibn Kathir** reads ayah 87 chiefly from the criminals' side — they will have nobody to plead for them. **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān**, following Rūḥ, reads it as defining who will be *permitted* to intercede. The rendering "none will have the right to intercede, except those who have taken a covenant" carries both. Either way, the two land in the same place: intercession is not owned or claimed, and the covenant is what stands a person in good place regarding it.

Note too that the same divine name governs both ends of the passage. The delegation is gathered **to al-Raḥmān** in ayah 85, and the covenant is taken **with al-Raḥmān** in ayah 87. The name of mercy is over both halves of this scene — and by the wording of ayah 87 itself, what one brings to it is a covenant.

## Living it

- **Check taqwā against the definition the sources give.** Ibn Kathir's description is a pattern, not a feeling: believing what the Messengers brought, obeying what they commanded, abstaining from what they prohibited.
- **Perfume the deed now.** In the narration Ibn Kathir cites, the fragrance the believer meets was applied "in the worldly life." The care you put into an act today is what meets you later.
- **Do not carry borrowed confidence in intercession.** The ayah denies that it is held or possessed. The one thing named as marking a person out is the covenant — and Ibn ʿAbbās's version of it ends with placing hope in Allah alone, which is the opposite of relying on someone else to fix it.
- **Renew the covenant, don't just remember it.** Ibn Kathir ties the testimony to "upholding of its rights and implications." The words begin the covenant; the life is the keeping of it.

passages.title: The claim that the Most Merciful has a son
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** These eight ayat answer the claim that Allah has taken a son — and they answer it not with a calm argument but with a picture of the universe itself flinching. The unit moves in one arc: the claim is reported (88), named for what it is (89), the creation recoils from it (90–91), it is shown to be beneath Allah's majesty (92), and then the true standing of every being before Allah is laid out — servanthood, being counted, and arriving alone (93–95).

## Where this falls in the sūrah

Ibn Kathir places it precisely. After Allah affirms in this noble sūrah that ʿĪsā was a worshipper and servant of Allah, and after mentioning his birth from Maryam without a father, He then begins refuting those who claim that He has a son — holy is He and far exalted above such a description. So this is not a new topic dropped in from nowhere. It follows directly on the account of ʿĪsā: having shown who the son of Maryam really was, the passage turns to the claim that people built on him.

The ayah just before (87) sets the hinge. It speaks of "the one who has taken a covenant (ʿahd) with al-Raḥmān." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports two readings of that covenant: Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās said it means a declaration of firm belief in the Oneness of Allah, while others said it means committing the Qur'an to memory. In short, only those who stand firm by their covenant to hold to the true faith will have permission to intercede (Rūḥ). On Ibn ʿAbbās's reading, then, ayah 87 draws its line at *tawḥīd* — the belief that Allah is one, with no partner and no peer. Ayah 88 shows us the people standing on the wrong side of that line.

## "They say" — then suddenly, "you"

Ayah 88 reports the claim at a distance: *wa qālū ittakhadha ar-Raḥmānu waladā* — "and they said: the Most Merciful has taken a son." Ayah 89 wheels around and speaks to them directly: *laqad jiʼtum shayʼan iddā*. Ibn Kathir glosses "indeed you have brought forth" as meaning "in this statement of yours." The report becomes an indictment; the speakers are put on the spot.

Notice, too, which name of Allah the passage keeps using. Not a name of power or punishment, but **al-Raḥmān** — the Most Merciful — four times over (88, 91, 92, 93). The claim is aimed at the very One whose defining relation to them is mercy, and the hadith quoted below dwells on exactly that: the One they speak against is the One sustaining them.

## The word *iddā*

Arabic can compress an entire verdict into one word, and here it does. Four of the great early authorities gloss *iddā* identically: Ibn Kathir reports that **Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah and Mālik all said it means "terrible."** Not mistaken, not unsupported — monstrous. English renders it "an outrageous claim," and even that is a whole phrase reaching after one short Arabic word.

Ibn Kathir adds a recitational note: it has been said that the word is pronounced *iddan*, *addan*, and *addan* with elongation on the first vowel. All three pronunciations are known; the first is the most popular. It is worth pausing on the sound itself. From ayah 88 straight through to ayah 95, every single ayah closes on the same clipped *-dā*: *waladā* (88), *iddā* (89), *haddā* (90), *waladā* (91), *waladā* (92), *ʿabdā* (93), *ʿaddā* (94), *fardā* (95). The passage hammers one note, and the ear feels the verdict before the mind has finished parsing it.

## Ayat 90–91: creation recoils

This is the heart of the passage. The response to the claim is not a debate but a picture of the cosmos under strain — and what strains it is a sentence someone spoke.

**Why does creation react at all?** Ibn Kathir explains that the heavens, earth and mountains almost tear apart *out of their high esteem for Allah*, when they hear this statement of wickedness coming from the Children of Adam. His reasoning is that these are creatures of Allah, and they are established upon His tawḥīd and upon the fact that there is no deity worthy of worship except Him: He has no partners, no peer, no child, no mate and no coequal; rather He is the One, the Self-Sufficient Master whom all creatures are in need of. The universe is not neutral about its Lord.

Ibn Jarīr reported from **Ibn ʿAbbās**: "Verily, the heavens, the earth, the mountains and all creatures — except for humans and jinn — are frightened by the associating of partners with Allah. Creation will almost cease existing before the association of partners with Allah, due to His Greatness."

Read that carefully. *Shirk* — associating partners with Allah — is something only humans and jinn can commit, and on this report they are the only two who do not shudder at it. Rock and sky register Allah's greatness in a way that the creature with the greater share of perception does not.

**The three verbs, each opened by an early authority.**

- *tafaṭṭur* (the heavens "almost burst") — **Ad-Daḥḥāk** said this means to be split apart into pieces due to the fear of the magnificence of Allah.
- *tanshaqq* (the earth "splits") — **ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam** said this is due to its anger on behalf of Allah, the Mighty and Sublime. Fear above, indignation below.
- *haddā* (the mountains "fall down crumbling") — **Ibn ʿAbbās** said it means to be torn down; **Saʿīd bin Jubayr** said *haddan* means some of it is broken by other parts of it in succession — a collapse that travels through the whole mass, one section bringing down the next.

**Do mountains really perceive?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the question head-on: these verses suggest that the earth, the mountains, and everything that grows on them possess a certain degree of knowledge and intelligence, though in their case these perceptions are not of the same extent as that bestowed on human beings. This, it says, explains why everything in the world glorifies Allah, as in *"and there is not a single thing that does not extol His purity and praise"* (17:44). The verses point to that very perception: to associate anything with Allah — especially to assert that He has children — is a sin that makes the earth and the mountains quake with fear. And it cites Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh Ibn ʿAbbās: except for humans, every created thing is terrified of any suggestion of association with Allah (Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī).

**And yet it says "almost."** *Takādu* — the heavens are on the very edge of bursting, and they do not. Ibn ʿAbbās's words carry the same restraint: creation will *almost* cease to exist. The hadith Ibn Kathir cites next speaks directly to Allah's own forbearance.

## From the Sunnah: no one is more patient

Imam Aḥmad reported from Abū Mūsā that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "There is no one more patient than Allah concerning something harmful that He hears. For verily, partners are associated with Him and a son is ascribed to Him, while He is the One Who gives them good health, protects them and sustains them."

Ibn Kathir notes that this narration is also recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, and that in one wording it reads: "...that they attribute a son to Him, while He is the One Who sustains them and gives them good health."

Set this beside ayah 90 and the two pictures answer each other. The claim is grave enough that, on Ibn Kathir's reading, inert matter is on the edge of tearing itself apart over it — and the hadith says that the One against whom it is spoken keeps on healing them, shielding them and sustaining them. The creation nearly breaks; its Maker is described as more patient than anyone. The mountains have less forbearance than the One they would crumble for.

## Ayah 92: "It does not befit"

*Wa mā yanbaghī li-r-Raḥmāni an yattakhidha waladā.* Ibn Kathir explains: it is not befitting of Him, nor is it appropriate for His lofty majesty and greatness; there is no coequal for Him in His creation, because all creatures are His slaves.

Notice the reason he gives. The denial does not rest on what did or did not happen; it rests on the fact that there is no coequal to be had — *because all creatures are His slaves*. That is why Ibn Kathir moves straight from ayah 92 into ayah 93: "This is why He says..."

## Ayat 93–95: three words that settle everything

The refutation ends by simply describing reality, and the description does the demolition.

**ʿabdā — "as a servant" (93).** "There is none in the heavens and the earth but comes unto the Most Gracious as a slave." Not most. Not most-except-a-few. The Arabic *in kullu… illā* is a closed net — a total negation with a single exception clause — so every being in the heavens and the earth arrives before al-Raḥmān in exactly one posture: that of an owned servant. And the sūrah has already placed ʿĪsā himself inside that category, since, as Ibn Kathir noted at the outset, it affirms that ʿĪsā was a worshipper and servant of Allah. On the Qur'an's own terms, arriving as a servant is not a demotion; it is simply what every created being does.

**ʿaddā — "counted precisely" (94).** Ibn Kathir: He knows their number from the time He created them until the Day of Resurrection — male and female, both the small and the large of them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that it means Allah has full knowledge of their doings. The doubling in the Arabic (*aḥṣāhum wa ʿaddahum ʿaddā*) matches that: a counting so complete that neither the small nor the large of them falls outside it.

**fardā — "alone" (95).** Ibn Kathir: "This means that there will be no helper for him and no one to save him, except Allah alone, Who has no partners. He judges His creatures as He wills, and He is the Most Just, Who does not do even an atom's weight of injustice. He will not wrong anyone."

Notice how 94 and 95 work as a pair. You arrive with nobody — no helper, no rescuer of your own choosing. But you arrive before One who counted you individually. Coming alone is not being lost in the crowd; it is standing in front of the only Judge who could never mistake who you are, and who, as Ibn Kathir says, will not wrong anyone by an atom's weight.

## The word that outweighs the heavens

Ibn ʿAbbās's comment on ayah 90 does not stop at the terror of shirk. He draws the hopeful inverse: just as the idolater does not benefit from his good deeds because of associating partners with Allah, we hope that Allah would forgive the sins of those who believed in His absolute Oneness by worshipping Him alone.

And within that same report of Ibn ʿAbbās — the one Ibn Kathir transmits from Ibn Jarīr — the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is quoted as saying:

> "Encourage your dying people to testify to *lā ilāha illallāh*, for whoever says it at the time of their death, they will definitely enter Paradise."

The people said: O Messenger of Allah, what about he who says it while in good health? He replied: "This will necessitate his entrance into Paradise even more." Then he said:

> "I swear by He Whom my soul is in His Hand, if the heavens and the earths, and all that is in them, between them and under them, were brought and placed in a balance of a scale, and the testimony of *lā ilāha illallāh* was placed on the other side of the scale, the testimony would outweigh all of it."

Ibn Kathir's own note on this is: "This was recorded by Ibn Jarir and it is supported by the Hadith related to the story of the card. And Allah knows best."

The symmetry with ayah 90 is striking: the same heavens, earth and mountains that nearly tear themselves apart when Allah's Oneness is violated are outweighed on the scale when it is affirmed. One sentence about Allah nearly undoes creation. Another sentence about Allah outweighs it.

## Living it

- **Weigh what you say about Allah.** The passage's whole force lands on a single short sentence that shook the sky. Careless speech about Allah, His nature, or what He "must" be like is not a small matter — the Qur'an's own word for this claim is *iddā*, which Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah and Mālik all glossed as "terrible."
- **Say the kalimah now, in good health.** The *kalimah* is the testimony *lā ilāha illallāh* — "there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah." In the narration above, the Prophet ﷺ was asked about exactly this case and answered that it necessitates Paradise "even more." Do not save it for the deathbed.
- **Prompt the dying gently with *lā ilāha illallāh*.** That is the instruction reported in the same narration for anyone sitting with someone at the end — a reminder, not a demand.
- **Let Allah's forbearance astonish you.** The Abū Mūsā hadith is a statement about Allah, not a lesson about us. The right first response is wonder: by its own words, the One who is spoken against is the same One giving good health, protection and sustenance.
- **Take *ʿabdā* as your identity (93).** No rank, no title and no lineage changes the posture in which anyone arrives. Whatever else you are, you are His servant.
- **Prepare for *fardā* (95).** Ibn Kathir's gloss is stark: no helper and no one to save him, except Allah alone. Nothing you can share, delegate or hide behind will be with you. What survives the journey is what was between you and Allah alone. Build that.

passages.title: Affection for the believers, and a warning to the hostile
passages.tafsir:
Surah Maryam closes with three ayat that belong together as one movement. The first tells us what Allah does for those who believe and act on their belief: He creates love for them. The second tells His Prophet ﷺ why this Qur'an came in his own tongue — glad tidings for one kind of listener, warning for another. The third points at the ground where whole nations used to stand and asks whether anything of them can still be seen or heard. One contrast runs through all three: the servant whose name is announced with love in the heavens and whose acceptance is then laid down on the earth, and the rejecter of whom, in the end, not even a whisper is left.

## The promise: a love that Allah Himself creates

Ibn Kathir gives the ayah as: *"Verily, those who believe and work deeds of righteousness, the Most Gracious will bestow love for them."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same words: *"Surely those who believe and do the righteous deeds, for them the Rahman (All-Merciful) will create love."*

Two things are asked of the servant here, and one thing is promised by Allah.

Asked: faith, and righteous deeds. Ibn Kathir is careful about what makes a deed righteous — they are deeds, he says, "that He is pleased with because they are in accordance with the legislation of Muhammad ﷺ." So it is not good intentions floating free of guidance, and not outward form emptied of faith. The ayah names both: *believe*, and *work deeds of righteousness*.

Promised: love. Notice who supplies it, and under which Name. The commentators render the Name here as the Most Gracious, the All-Merciful, the Most Compassionate — Allah gives this gift under the Name of His mercy. And He is the one who gives it. The believer is nowhere told to make himself likeable, to campaign for reputation, or to manage how he is seen. He is told to believe and to do good. Ibn Kathir says that Allah "plants love for them in the hearts of His righteous servants," and he states it as a settled law rather than a hopeful possibility: "This is something that is absolutely necessary and there is no avoiding it. This has been reported in authentic Hadiths of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in various different ways."

## How that love travels: from above the heavens down to the earth

The hadith Ibn Kathir brings shows the route it takes, and it is worth following step by step. Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Hurayrah said that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Verily, whenever Allah loves a servant of His, He calls Jibril and says, 'O Jibril, verily I love so-and-so, so love him.' Thus, Jibril will love him. Then, he (Jibril) will call out to the dwellers of the heavens, 'Verily, Allah loves so-and-so, so you too must love him.' Then the dwellers of the heavens love him and he will be given acceptance in the earth."

Ibn Kathir notes that **Al-Bukhari and Muslim** reported narrations similar to this.

Read the sequence again. It begins with Allah's love, not with the servant's standing among people. It passes to Jibril, then to the dwellers of the heavens, and only at the very end does it touch the ground we walk on — *"and he will be given acceptance in the earth."* In the order the hadith describes, human acceptance comes last. It is not the thing the servant is told to pursue; it is the last link in a chain whose first link is above the sky.

Ibn Kathir cites a second narration of Abu Hurayrah, recorded by **Ibn Abi Hatim**, in which the Prophet ﷺ described this same descent — Allah calls Jibril, Jibril calls out into the heavens, "and love for him descends among the people of the earth" — and then recited *this very ayah* as its meaning: "That is the meaning of the statement of Allah, the Mighty and Sublime: *Verily, those who believe and work deeds of righteousness, the Most Gracious will bestow love for them.*" Ibn Kathir adds that this was also reported by **Muslim and At-Tirmidhi**, and that At-Tirmidhi said, "Hasan Sahih."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates the hadith too, on the authority of Sayyidna Abu Hurairah, attributing it to **Bukhari, Tirmidhi and others** (citing Ruh ul-Maʿani), and likewise notes that the Prophet ﷺ then quoted this verse.

That detail matters: we are not stretching the ayah to fit a hadith. The Prophet ﷺ himself attached the two together.

## The same announcement, in reverse

The hadith Imam Ahmad recorded does not stop at love. It continues:

> "Whenever Allah hates a servant of His, He calls Jibril and says, 'O Jibril, verily I hate so-and-so, so hate him.' Thus, Jibril will hate him. Then, he (Jibril) will call out amongst the dwellers of the heavens, 'Verily, Allah hates so-and-so, so you too must hate him.' Then the dwellers of the heavens hate him and hatred for him will be placed in the earth."

Hold that second half in mind, because the two ayat that follow do exactly the same thing — they set glad tidings and warning side by side, in that order, and then show us where each road ends.

## What this love looks like on the ground

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out two visible effects of the promise in ayah 96.

**First, love among the believers themselves.** For those who are steadfast in their faith in Him, Allah "creates an environment of friendship and love for each other, which consequently promotes mutual amity and goodwill among the true Muslims." So the ayah is not only about an individual becoming beloved; it is about a community being knit together. Where faith and righteous action are real, warmth between believers is not a fragile achievement of good manners — it is something Allah creates among them.

**Second, respect from beyond that circle.** Maʿārif adds that by their conduct and behaviour such people "command the admiration and respect of all those with whom they come into contact." Character is the visible edge of this gift; people who deal with a believer feel it before they can name it.

Maʿārif also quotes Haram bin Hayyan, by way of Qurtubi: when a person "devotes himself wholly towards Allah He fills the hearts of all believers with love for him." Note the direction of the exchange — the servant turns fully to Allah; Allah turns hearts toward the servant. Reversing it, turning to people in the hope of winning them, is not what the ayah describes.

## Ibrahim's duʿā, still being answered

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a striking illustration. Sayyidna Ibrahim Khalilullah (peace be upon him), in accordance with the command of Allah, left his wife Hajira and his baby son Sayyidna Ismaʿil (peace be upon him) in the desert enclosed by the barren hills of Makkah; and when he planned to go back to Syria, he prayed for them both:

> *"So make hearts of a number of people yearn toward them."* (14:37)

The prayer was granted. Maʿārif observes that even after the lapse of many millennia, people all over the world entertain great love for Makkah and its inhabitants — visiting in large numbers, incurring heavy expenditure and enduring great hardships to make the journey. That is what it looks like when Allah creates love for someone: a family left alone in a barren place with nothing, and hearts pulled toward that spot ever since.

## The same Qur'an, two hearings

*"So, We have made this easy in your own tongue, only that you may give glad tidings to those who have Taqwa, and warn with it the people that are Ludda."*

Ibn Kathir explains "**We have made this easy**" as referring to the Qur'an, and "**in your own tongue**" as an address to Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, meaning that the Qur'an is "in the pure, complete and eloquent Arabic language." The revelation was not delivered in a locked or foreign idiom to be decoded by specialists. It came in the clearest tongue, on the tongue of the man sent to recite it.

Then the ayah names its two purposes — and they fall in the same order, and along the same divide, as the two halves of the hadith above.

- **Glad tidings** — for *al-muttaqin*, those who have taqwa (the mindful fear of Allah that keeps a person on His path). Ibn Kathir defines them here in the plainest terms: "those who respond to Allah and believe in His Messenger ﷺ." By that definition, taqwa begins with answering the call when it comes.
- **Warning** — for *qawman luddā*. Ibn Kathir explains the *Ludda* as "the people who have deviated away from the truth and are inclined towards falsehood."

Two audiences, one recitation. The very same Arabic that comforts the responsive unsettles the hostile. And this sits directly after the promise of love: the believer for whom that love is being announced, and the obstinate opponent, are both hearing the same words in the same clear tongue.

## Where the other road ends

*"And how many a generation before them have We destroyed! Can you find a single one of them or hear even a whisper of them?"*

Ibn Kathir identifies the destroyed generations as "the nations that disbelieved in the signs of Allah and rejected His Messengers." So the warning of the previous ayah is not an abstract threat; it has a history behind it, and Allah invites the listener to go and look for its remains.

The question is put to two senses. Ibn Kathir gives the meaning as, "have you seen any of them or even heard a whisper from them." Al-Hasan and Qatadah both said that this means, "Do you see with your eye, or hear any sound?" As for the "whisper" — *rikz* — Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Al-ʿAliyah, ʿIkrimah, Al-Hasan Al-Basri, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Ad-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd all said, "This means any sound."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens it further: the word means "a faint, unintelligible sound such as a death-rattle." So the bar is set as low as language allows. Not a kingdom, not a monument, not a spokesman, not even a voice — just the faintest noise a body can make. And there is none.

Maʿārif then draws the lesson plainly: there have been many kings who ruled vast empires, exercised unlimited authority and lived in great splendour, "but when the wrath of Allah caught upon them for their sinful acts, they were annihilated in such a manner that not even a whisper or a feeble motion is now being heard of them."

## The three together

Set the two ends of the passage side by side and the argument completes itself.

The believer of the first ayah does nothing to advertise himself — and Allah has love for him announced in the heavens and acceptance laid down for him on the earth, permanently, "absolutely necessary and there is no avoiding it."

The kings of the last ayah had everything a person could want announced about them: empire, unlimited authority, splendour. Go and listen for them now. Not a sound.

Between the two stands the middle ayah and the Qur'an itself, made easy in a clear tongue, still doing both of its jobs at once — glad tidings to whoever will respond, warning to whoever will not. Which half of that ayah is addressed to us is settled by the same two conditions the passage opened with: believing, and doing righteous deeds — deeds, as Ibn Kathir specified, in accordance with the legislation of Muhammad ﷺ.

**Living it.** The practical instruction is almost the opposite of what we assume. Do not work at being loved; work at faith and at deeds done the way the Messenger ﷺ taught. Acceptance on earth is Allah's to place, and in this ayah He has undertaken it. And if you find yourself genuinely loved by the righteous, receive it as something that came down to you rather than something you achieved — the hadith traces every link of that chain back to Allah.

*This is the end of the Tafsir of Surah Maryam. All praises and thanks are due to Allah.*
